source.title: Steer2Edit: From Activation Steering to Component-Level Editing
source.authors: Chung-En Sun; Ge Yan; Zimo Wang; T. Weng

record.file_problem: The text contains the paper and appendices. The code URL is truncated in the text.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses mean-difference steering vectors and adds them to intermediate activations, then reports refusal and utility outcomes. This bears on the vector’s ability to affect refusal, but the vector construction and tested outcomes do not reproduce the single-direction ablation and harmless-request tests in V1.
record.gate_note: The study reports activation-steering safety–utility curves for the claim-relevant refusal behavior. The safety direction is constructed from refusal responses to harmful prompts minus helpful responses to benign questions. Other reported results concern the paper’s component-level editing method or other behaviors and are not included as rows for these claim versions.
record.test_reason: This is a methods paper. It takes mean-difference steering vectors as an off-the-shelf tool, converts them into component-level rank-1 weight edits (Steer2Edit), and reports that method's safety–utility trade-off against an activation-steering baseline. The safety vector is not the V1 recipe: it is built per layer and per block from response-token activations (refusal responses to harmful prompts minus helpful responses to Alpaca prompts). It is added at every block with strength γ, and evaluated only on jailbreak-transformed harmful prompts. The steering baseline appears only as unlabelled curves in Figures 2, 8 and 14, with no stated values. The study does no ablation, does not induce refusal on harmless prompts, and does not ask whether one direction mediates refusal. Its results therefore concern its own method's performance, not whether any claim version holds.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that steering vectors work as diagnostic signals that can be turned into sparse, closed-form, component-level rank-1 weight edits. These edits give better attribute–utility trade-offs than activation steering for safety, truthfulness and reasoning efficiency. They make no claim about whether a single direction mediates refusal.
record.recipe_differences: Uses mean differences and inference-time activation addition, but builds separate vectors for each layer and attention/MLP block from generated response activations. It does not perform the claimed all-layer, all-position projection ablation or test refusal on harmless requests.
record.method_sensitivity: Activation-steering strength γ; jailbreak attack type (GCG versus ADV-LLM) and downstream utility dataset are also evaluated separately in Appendix D.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding layer- and block-specific refusal-response steering vectors raises refusal against GCG and ADV-LLM jailbreaks on LLaMA-2-7B-Chat and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2. Strong steering brings substantial utility loss on GSM8K, CodeMMLU and CommonsenseQA (figure only).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Steering with a response-derived refusal vector strengthens jailbreak refusal, at a utility cost that grows with strength.

fits_no_version.finding: Steer2Edit's safety edits are sparse and concentrate on a few late-layer attention heads. Varying the attention budget alone drives refusal gains, while MLP-only edits give weak gains (Figures 3 and 11).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal strengthening along a steering direction is carried mainly by a small set of late-layer attention heads.

record.problems: The safety results are shown as figures without exact plotted values or uncertainty estimates in the text. The refusal evaluation covers two models and harmful jailbreak prompts; benign-task accuracy is an aggregate proxy for capability. The tested vectors are layer- and block-specific, and the study does not test removal of refusal by ablation.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-version rows retained. Appendix D separates attack and utility-dataset trade-offs, but does not provide exact values in the text; the main aggregate safety–utility results are represented in r1–r4.
record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests'/T2 classification and the V1 limits_scope label are withdrawn. The steering baseline is a comparator for the paper's own method, built with a different direction construction and shown only in figures, so no verdict on V1 can rest on it. Arditi et al. is cited only as prior steering work. The reasoning-model experiments (Qwen3-4B-Thinking) concern reasoning length, not refusal, so they do not bear on V8.

versions.untested_parts: Does not ablate the direction; does not test whether one direction is unique or whether projecting it out at every layer and position removes refusal; does not test addition causing refusal to harmless requests. Uses separate layer- and block-specific directions and reports aggregate utility on three benchmarks.
The study edits weights to strengthen safety; it does not test abliteration or removal of refusal in released models.
It evaluates GCG and ADV-LLM jailbreaks but does not test whether they work by suppressing the refusal direction, or train against direction ablation.
It does not compare a single direction with affine, cone, or multiple-direction accounts of refusal.
It does not separately measure harmfulness judgment and refusal decision.
It does not test transfer across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct models.
It compares training-based methods for behavioral control but does not test whether refusal-training choices determine whether a removable direction exists.
It evaluates reasoning efficiency in reasoning models, not whether the refusal direction mechanism holds in them.
